title: Job 26:5–14
context: In the book as it stands, Job continues speaking (26:1) with a hymn on the edges of God’s ways. The poem moves from the realm of the dead, where the departed spirits tremble and Sheol and Abaddon lie open before God (26:5–6), through the heavens, the earth, the clouds, and the boundary of the waters (26:7–10), to God’s mastery over the sea, Rahab, and the swift serpent (26:11–13). It ends by confessing that all this is only “the outskirts of his ways,” that only a whisper is heard of him, while “the thunder of his power” is beyond understanding (26:14). Some readers propose that 26:5–14 continues Bildad’s speech from chapter 25, since it extends his theme of God’s majesty; others read it as Job outdoing Bildad on his own theme, showing that he knows God’s greatness at least as well. The book as it stands assigns the passage to Job, and these notes present both views without deciding between them. The imagery draws on poetic language for creation and its powers: Rahab here, as in 9:13, is not the woman of Jericho but is generally taken as a poetic name for a sea monster or power of chaos subdued by God, and the swift serpent is often linked with similar imagery (compare 3:8; Isaiah 27:1), though the background is debated. Both Arminian and Reformed readers read the hymn as doxology, neither pressing its cosmic pictures into modern scientific statements nor dismissing them as mere error, and both see it pointing ahead to the LORD’s speeches in chapters 38–41.

verses.text: “The departed spirits tremble, those beneath the waters and all that live in them.
verses.arminianNotes: The hymn opens in the depths: the departed spirits tremble, those beneath the waters and all that live in them. Some readers think the poem here resumes Bildad’s speech, while the text as it stands continues Job’s. Arminian readers hear a confession that no realm, not even the place of the dead, lies outside God’s presence and reach.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the trembling of the departed as a picture of God’s sovereign rule extending even below the world of the living (compare Psalm 139:8). The precise identity of the “departed spirits” in Israel’s poetry is debated. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as doxology about God’s reach, not as a detailed map of the afterlife.

verses.text: Sheol is naked before God, and Abaddon has no covering.
verses.arminianNotes: Job says Sheol, the place of the dead, is naked before God, and Abaddon, the place of destruction, has no covering (compare Proverbs 15:11). Arminian readers note that Job, who earlier spoke of Sheol as a hiding place (14:13), now confesses that nothing there is hidden from God, and they find comfort that God’s knowledge reaches every condition.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers stress God’s exhaustive knowledge, from which nothing in creation, even the realm of the dead, is concealed (compare Hebrews 4:13). How Israel’s poets pictured Sheol and Abaddon is variously understood. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as confessing God’s total knowledge, while holding the details of the imagery with care.

verses.text: He stretches out the north over empty space, and hangs the earth on nothing.
verses.arminianNotes: Job says God stretches out the north over empty space and hangs the earth on nothing. Some readers hear in “the north” a reference to the heights associated with divine dwelling in the region’s poetry, though this is debated. Arminian readers take the line as a confession that creation rests on God’s power alone, without pressing it into a scientific claim.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God upholding all things by his word (compare Hebrews 1:3), and they read the image as praise for the Creator who needs no foundation beyond himself. Shared ground: both traditions hold that the verse confesses God’s sustaining power in poetic terms; they neither turn it into modern cosmology nor dismiss it as simple error.

verses.text: He binds up the waters in his thick clouds, and the cloud is not burst under them.
verses.arminianNotes: Job marvels that God binds up the waters in his thick clouds without the cloud bursting under them. Arminian readers see in the everyday wonder of rain held in the sky a sign of God’s faithful care for the world, which they connect with his kindness in sending rain on all people (compare Acts 14:17).
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers read the image as evidence of God’s providential ordering of the weather, a theme the LORD himself raises when he asks Job who can number the clouds (38:37). Shared ground: both traditions take the verse as praise for God’s sustaining care in ordinary things, described poetically rather than technically.

verses.text: He encloses the face of his throne, and spreads his cloud on it.
verses.arminianNotes: Job says God encloses the face of his throne and spreads his cloud on it. Arminian readers hear a confession that God is both near in his works and hidden in his majesty, and they note that this hiddenness fits Job’s earlier complaint that he cannot find God (23:8–9), even while he still believes God reigns.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the cloud around God’s throne as a sign of his transcendence and holiness, a theme found elsewhere in Scripture (compare Psalm 97:2). Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as confessing that God rules from a throne humans cannot see, and both hear in it an echo of Job’s experience of God’s hiddenness.

verses.text: He has described a boundary on the surface of the waters, and to the confines of light and darkness.
verses.arminianNotes: Job says God has described a boundary on the surface of the waters, to the confines of light and darkness. Arminian readers see the image of God setting limits to the sea and marking the border of day and night (compare Proverbs 8:27–29), and they hear assurance that chaos is never left unbounded in God’s world.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the close link with the LORD’s later question about who shut up the sea and set its bars (38:8–11), and they stress that God’s decree fixes the bounds of every created power. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as poetic praise for God’s ordering of creation, without treating it as a technical description of the horizon.

verses.text: The pillars of heaven tremble and are astonished at his rebuke.
verses.arminianNotes: Job says the pillars of heaven tremble and are astonished at God’s rebuke. Arminian readers treat the pillars as poetic imagery for the foundations of the sky, as with the pillars of the earth in 9:6, and they see the whole created order responding to God’s voice, not a scientific claim about how the heavens are built.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise take the pillars as poetic imagery and read the verse as a confession that the strongest parts of creation tremble at God’s word (compare Psalm 104:7). Shared ground: both traditions read the line as doxology about God’s authority over creation, and both decline to press the imagery literally.

verses.text: He stirs up the sea with his power, and by his understanding he strikes through Rahab.
verses.arminianNotes: Job says God stirs up the sea with his power and by his understanding strikes through Rahab. Arminian readers note that this Rahab is not the woman of Jericho but, as generally understood, a poetic name for a sea monster or power of chaos (compare 9:13; Psalm 89:10), and they hold the background of the image loosely.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise take Rahab here as poetic imagery for a chaos power subdued by God, noting Isaiah 51:9, where some readers also hear Egypt. They stress that God’s power and wisdom act together. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as praise for God’s mastery over every threatening power, while hedging the image’s precise background.

verses.text: By his Spirit the heavens are garnished. His hand has pierced the swift serpent.
verses.arminianNotes: Job says that by God’s Spirit the heavens are garnished and his hand has pierced the swift serpent. Many readers link the serpent with leviathan imagery (compare 3:8; Isaiah 27:1), though the background is debated. Arminian readers hear a confession that God both adorns creation and defeats whatever opposes his good order.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that WEB’s “Spirit” recalls God’s Spirit at creation (compare Genesis 1:2; Psalm 33:6), and some read the line in light of later Trinitarian teaching while recognizing that Job’s horizon is more limited. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as doxology about God’s creative and conquering power, hedging the serpent’s identity.

verses.text: Behold, these are but the outskirts of his ways. How small a whisper do we hear of him! But the thunder of his power who can understand?”
verses.arminianNotes: Job ends the hymn by saying these are but the outskirts of God’s ways, a small whisper, while the thunder of his power is beyond understanding. Arminian readers hear humility and wonder, and they note that Job’s confession prepares for the LORD’s speeches, where God reveals more of his ways while still leaving Job in awe (38–41).
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers stress the incomprehensibility of God: humans know him truly but never exhaustively, and what is revealed is a whisper beside the whole (compare Romans 11:33). Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as the climax of the hymn, confessing God’s greatness beyond human grasp, whichever speaker the passage is assigned to.
